newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 11.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- LONDON OPENS HOUSE PRICE GAP

The latest survey from the Halifax Building Society show that London house prices are accelerating at their fastest pace in ten years and a 1980s-style gulf is beginning to open up between the North and South. A similar pattern to London has been developing in the South. Gary Marsh, housing analyst at Halifax, said that the housing market in London was different to that elsewhere in the country. Estate agents reported that a shortage of properties is pushing prices up.
-- SAUDI PRINCE IN LONRHO HOTELS COUP

Prince al-Waleed is set to win most of Lonrho's Princess luxury hotels for 440 million dollars. The properties had been expected to fetch between 350 and 400 million stg and Lonrho are understood to be very disappointed. The deal involves 140 million dollars in cash from the Prince and 220 million dollars from a consortium of banks led by HSBC with the remaining 80 million dollars coming in a loan from Lonrho.
-- CITY SEES RATES RISING SOON AFTER POLLING DAY

Analysts warn that interest rates are set to rise between a quarter and a half point after the general election. This follows a policy meeting between Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Eddie George, governor of the Bank of England, which broke up without an announcement. However, City analysts believe the governor will redouble his efforts to secure a rate rise once the election is over.
THE TIMES
-- UTILITIES SHARES BOOSTED BY MODEST WINDFALL TAX HOPES

The Labour Party will today include windfall tax as a key element of an election manifesto for business. Expectations that the tax will be more modest than the City had originally feared has led to a rise in utilities shares. Also, in a statement on the future of UK telecommunications, the main telecommunications unions, the Communication Workers Union and the Society of Telecom Executives, called for Labour to reduce the impact of windfall tax on British Telecom.
-- BLAIR PLEDGE TO REVITALISE PFI GOALS

The Labour Party is set to unveil its plans to revitalise the Private Finance Initiative. This is the first evidence of a closer public-private partnership in government. The move will come in Labour's election manifesto for business being launched in the City today, called 'Equipping Britain for the Future'. Labour's 12-point plan for the PFI will form one of the five key pledges Tony Blair and Shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown will make to business leaders.
-- NATWEST MAY OFFER GAS TO CUSTOMERS

NatWest is to link with Eastern Group, part of The Energy Group, to offer more than six million customers gas and electricity. Eastern will initially market energy to bank employees and their relatives in areas of southern England where gas is sold competitively. Eastern is offering gas tariffs and NatWest receives payment for each customer recruited. NatWest said the arrangement will benefit the bank and its employees financially.
THE GUARDIAN
-- STUDENTS FACE BOOKS CHAOS

Publishers and university leaders are locked in a row over copyright fees. If the dispute is not resolved this summer thousands of higher education students could be denied access to vital academic texts. The two sides have been lobbying Sir Ron Dearing to recommend a solution in his forthcoming interim review of higher education provisions. According to the Publishers' Association, the outcome will affect the entire structure of academic publishing.
-- PROPOSAL FOR STATE ACCESS TO COMPANY COMPUTERS

According to Department of Trade proposals, firms should use government-licenced organisations to provide them with computer security codes for electronic commerce. Security and intelligence agencies will have to know private encryption codes of Trusted Third Parties, which provide encryption services to companies trading through communications systems such as the Internet. The agencies are concerned about the use of encoded communications by drug-traffickers, money-launderers and other criminals.
-- IMRO FINES LINCOLN INSURANCE GROUP 20,000 STG

Life insurance group, Lincoln, has been fined 20,000 stg by the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation, the City watchdog, and ordered to pay costs of 30,000 stg for rule breaches at its fund management arm. Imro said the fine related to the late banking of client money and inadequate monitoring procedures in its personal equity plan business. The low level of penalty reflects the fact that no client was left out of pocket and that Lincoln reported the problem itself.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- CO-OP COST-CUTTING PLAN TO SAVE MILLIONS

The Co-operative Wholesale Society is planning a cost cutting programme which will make the business more efficient. Graham Melmoth, chief executive, had set up working parties to cut costs when he took over last autumn. CWS denied the plans were in response to Andrew Regan's Lanica Trust's aim to cut ten million stg from the society's central costs if its attempt to acquire parts of the division's non-food businesses proved successful.
-- LABOUR TO CALL WATER SUMMIT

Environmental spokesman for the Labour Party, Frank Dobson, has pledged to call an immediate post-poll industry summit on water shortages. This is a clear signal that it would introduce a tougher regulatory regime on the privatised water companies. The party is attempting to turn growing fears of a summer drought crisis into an election issue. Dobson outlined a 10-point list of measures as several water companies are already warning of the possibility of a drought.
-- ROLLS TO DOUBLE ANNUAL BONUSES

Aero-engine manufacturer, Rolls-Royce, has decided to double annual bonus payments for top executives because its scheme is no longer competitive with comparable companies. Executive directors will now be able to earn annual bonuses equivalent to 40 percent of their basic salary. Rolls' annual report and accounts discloses that the company is replacing its executive share options scheme with a long-term incentive plan.
